blocks.text: B1-23 · Spontaneous conversation guided
Lesson overview

So far you have spoken mainly with prepared dialogues, role-playing games and presentations. To Layer B1 you must be able to support a spontaneous conversation on family issues: answer unexpected questions, ask for clarification, express an opinion, agree or not, and especially do not block yourself when you miss a word. In this unit Luke is in Cairo, at the summer course: he speaks in Arabic standard with an Egyptian teacher and with companions from other countries, and with Laylā, arrived from Lebanon for a conference. Learn compensation strategies (description something you don't know the name of), formulas to ask, verify, take time, interrupt, agree and disagree, and natural passage between fuṣḥā and dialect. Three weeks, with many conversation sessions.

rows: B1 · Module B1.4 "Write, speak, open sources"
18–20 hours · three weeks (weeks 145–147), plus the EGY track

blocks.text: Materials This unit, argument-cards (section 9), recorder, at least four conversation sessions with the tutor or Arabic partner
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. describe an object or concept you don't know the name of ( ⁧الشَّيْءُ الَّذِي⁩ …, ⁧نَوْعٌ مِنْ⁩ …);
2. ask to repeat, explain, speak more slowly, and verify that you understand;
3. take time, hold and give up the shift, cut off with courtesy;
4. express agreement, disagreement and doubt in a gradual and courteous manner;
5. support a conversation of 8–10 minutes on a familiar theme, passing between fuṣḥā and dialect when It's okay, it's okay. Three-week plan.

1. Dialogue 1 · What's that thing called?
Cairo, a language institute. Time of conversation with the professor Maǧdī. With Luca there are Miguel, a Spanish student, and Yōko, a Japanese student.

rows: ⁧مَجْدِي: صَبَاحَ الخَيْرِ! اليَوْمَ سَاعَةُ المُحَادَثَةِ: لَا كُتُبَ وَلَا دَفَاتِرَ. يُوكُو، اِسْأَلِي لُوكَا عَنْ أُسْبُوعِهِ الأَوَّلِ فِي القَاهِرَةِ.⁩
MaǧdīMorning! Today is the time of conversation: no books or notebooks. YōkoAsk Luke about his first week in Cairo.
⁧كَيْفَ⁩ … ⁧مُدْهِشًا، وَمُتْعِبًا قَلِيلًا. فِي اليَوْمِ الثَّانِي تَعَطَّلَ⁩ … ⁧كَانَ⁩ : ⁧لُوكَا⁩ ⁧أَقُولُ؟ الجِهَازُ الَّذِي يُسَخِّنُ المَاءَ فِي الحَمَّامِ.⁩
Luca: It was... amazing, and a little tiring. The second day broke... what do you say? The water heater in the bathroom.
⁧مَجْدِي: السَّخَّانُ! بِالفُصْحَى وَبِالعَامِّيَّةِ: سَخَّانٌ. أَحْسَنْتَ يَا لُوكَا: عِنْدَمَا لَا تَعْرِفُ الكَلِمَةَ، صِفِ الشَّيْءَ.⁩
MaǧdīThe water heater! In fuṣḥā and in dialect: saḫḫān. Bravo, Luca: When you don't know the word, describe it.
⁧ذٰلِكَ الشَّيْءَ⁩ … ⁧وَأَنَا أَفْعَلُ ذٰلِكَ دَائِمًا! أَمْسِ أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَشْتَرِيَ⁩ : ⁧مِيغِيل⁩ … ⁧لِلشَّمْسِ، الَّذِي نَضَعُهُ عَلَى الجِلْدِ⁩
I always do that too! Yesterday, I wanted to buy that sunny thing that we put on our skin...
Yōko: A cream that protects from the sun?
⁧رَائِعٌ، أَنْتُمْ تُسَاعِدُونَ بَعْضُكُمْ بَعْضًا.⁩ .« ⁧وَاقِي الشَّمْسِ⁩ » ⁧نَعَمْ:⁩ : ⁧مَجْدِي⁩ ⁧يُوكُو، وَأَنْتِ؟ مَا الَّذِي فَاجَأَكِ فِي القَاهِرَةِ؟⁩
Maǧdī: Yes: Sunscreen is the sunscreen. Great, you help each other. Yōko- What about you? What surprised you in Cairo?
⁧هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تَقُولَهَا بِكَلِمَاتٍ⁩ .« ⁧فَاجَأَكِ⁩ » ⁧عُذْرًا، لَمْ أَفْهَمْ كَلِمَةَ⁩ : ⁧يُوكُو⁩ ⁧أُخْرَى؟⁩
Yōko: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the word "I"fāǧaʾaki». Can you say that in other words?
Maǧdī: Sure: what didn't you expect?
⁧وَبِكَرَمِ النَّاسِ.⁩ … ⁧آه، مَفْهُومٌ! بِصَرَاحَةٍ، فُوجِئْتُ بِالضَّجِيجِ⁩ : ⁧يُوكُو⁩ ⁧صَاحِبُ الدُّكَّانِ تَحْتَ بَيْتِي لَا يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ مِنِّي نُقُودًا عَلَى الشَّايِ!⁩
Yōko: Ah, of course! Frankly, I was surprised by the noise and generosity of people. The shop owner under the house doesn't want to get paid for tea!
⁧لُوكَا: هٰذَا صَحِيحٌ! وَأَنَا فُوجِئْتُ بِأَنَّ النَّاسَ يَفْهَمُونَ الفُصْحَى، لٰكِنَّهُمْ يُجِيبُونَ بِالعَامِّيَّةِ.⁩
It's true! And I was surprised that people understood the fuṣḥā, but answers in dialect.
⁧مَجْدِي: هٰذِهِ هِيَ القَاهِرَةُ: لُغَتَانِ فِي حِوَارٍ وَاحِدٍ! وَأَنْتُمُ الآنَ تَتَكَلَّمُونَ بِلَا خَجَلٍ، وَهٰذَا هُوَ المُهِمُّ.⁩
Maǧdī: This is Cairo: two languages in one conversation! And now you speak without shyness, and that's what matters.

blocks.text: What to notice. Strategies: Luke describes the object he cannot name ( ⁧الجِهَازُ الَّذِي يُسَخِّنُ المَاءَ⁩ ); Miguel does the same ( ⁧ذٰلِكَ الشَّيْءَ⁩ … ⁧الَّذِي نَضَعُهُ عَلَى الجِلْدِ⁩ ); Yōko calls for reformulation ( ⁧هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تَقُولَهَا بِكَلِمَاتٍ أُخْرَى؟⁩ ) and confirms that it has understood ( ⁧مَفْهُومٌ⁩ !). ⁧كَيْفَ أَقُولُ؟⁩ It's a time-taking task. ⁧الجِلْد⁩ The skin is not exposed to the skin. ⁧الضَّجِيج⁩ The noise of the vehicle shall be: ⁧الكَرَم⁩ • generosity • ⁧الدُّكَّان⁩ The shop is in. ⁧بَعْضُكُمْ بَعْضًا⁩ "At each other" is equal to "At each other."
2. What is a spontaneous conversation

In a real conversation you don't know what they're gonna ask you; You're missing a word out of ten; The other one talks faster about your book and sometimes goes to the dialect. It's not a grammar test: it's a collaboration. It matters that the message passes, that you know how to fix when something doesn't work and that the other one wants to keep talking to you. The fuṣḥā as a common language. With a teacher, with foreign students, with Arabs from different countries (a Lebanese and a Moroccan, for example), fuṣḥā is the common ground. In educated conversations one uses a fuṣḥā simplified: short sentences, few pronounced cases, many common words to dialects. This is the language of the dialogues of this unity.
3. When a word is missing

rows: What do you say? - What's his name?

blocks.text: say the word in another language ... ⁧بِالإِنْجِلِيزِيَّةِ نَقُولُ⁩ In English, we say...

⁧مُسْتَدِير⁩ Round ⁧البْلَاسْتِيك⁩ The plastic is the same as the plastic. The last resource, the word in another language, often works with young people and educated people; but first try to describe: this is how the vocabulary grows, because the other will tell you the right word.
4. Understand and make yourself understood

rows: Excuse me, can you repeat that?
What does that mean? · What do you mean by...?
Can you say that in other words?

blocks.text: correct a misunderstanding ... ⁧لَا، لَمْ أَقْصِدْ ذٰلِكَ. قَصَدْتُ أَنَّ⁩ No, that's not what I meant. I meant that...
Verify is courteous. Repeat with your own words what you have understood ( ⁧تَقْصِدُ أَنَّ⁩ … ⁧؟⁩ ) avoids ⁧سُوءُ تَفَاهُمٍ⁩ • misunderstanding and show the other that you listen to him.
5. Take time and keep the shift

Take time. ⁧يَعْنِي⁩ … · ⁧فِي الحَقِيقَةِ⁩ … · ⁧كَيْفَ أَقُولُ؟⁩ · ⁧سُؤَالٌ جَيِّدٌ!⁩ · ⁧دَعْنِي أُفَكِّرُ قَلِيلًا⁩ . One of these formulas gives two or three seconds to think and tells the other that you're not finished. Hold and give up the shift.

rows: What do you think? · And you?
⁧حَسَنًا، يَجِبُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ الآنَ. فُرْصَةٌ سَعِيدَةٌ!⁩
All right, I gotta go. Nice to meet you.

blocks.text: 6. Dialogue 2 · A coffee with Laylā
Laylā He's in Cairo for a reporter's conference. She and Luca finally meet in person at a coffee shop in Zamalek.

rows: ⁧لَيْلَى: لُوكَا! أَخِيرًا نَلْتَقِي وَجْهًا لِوَجْهٍ، لَا عَلَى الشَّاشَةِ!⁩
LaylāLuca! We're finally meeting face to face, not on the screen!
⁧لَيْلَى: مُفِيدٌ، لٰكِنَّهُ طَوِيلٌ: خَمْسُ سَاعَاتٍ مِنَ الكَلِمَاتِ الرَّسْمِيَّةِ! قُلْ لِي، مَا انْطِبَاعُكَ عَنِ القَاهِرَةِ هٰذِهِ المَرَّةَ؟⁩
Laylā: Useful, but long: five hours of official talks! Tell me, what does Cairo make this time?
⁧لُوكَا: أَفْهَمُ أَكْثَرَ بِكَثِيرٍ مِنَ الصَّيْفِ المَاضِي. وَلِهٰذَا أَظُنُّ أَنَّ قَرَارِي كَانَ صَحِيحًا: الفُصْحَى أَوَّلًا، ثُمَّ اللَّهْجَةُ.⁩
Luca: I understand much more than last summer. That is why I believe that my decision was right: first the fuṣḥā, then the dialect.
⁧لَيْلَى: هُنَا لَا أَتَّفِقُ مَعَكَ تَمَامًا. فِي رَأْيِي، اللَّهْجَةُ أَوَّلًا، لِأَنَّهَا لُغَةُ الحَيَاةِ اليَوْمِيَّةِ. مَنْ يَبْدَأُ بِالفُصْحَى يَتَكَلَّمُ مِثْلَ نَشْرَةِ الأَخْبَارِ!⁩
Laylā: I don't agree entirely with you here. In my opinion the dialect first, because it is the language of everyday life. Who starts from fuṣḥā He's talking like a news show!
⁧لُوكَا: أَفْهَمُ وِجْهَةَ نَظَرِكِ، لٰكِنِ اسْمَحِي لِي: بِالفُصْحَى أَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ أَقْرَأَ الصُّحُفَ، وَأَنْ أَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَ العَرَبِ كُلِّهِمْ، مِنَ المَغْرِبِ إِلَى العِرَاقِ.⁩
Luca: I understand your point of view, but allow me: with the fuṣḥā I can read the papers and talk to all Arabs, from Morocco to Iraq.
Laylā: True, but on the street...
⁧لُوكَا: عُذْرًا عَلَى المُقَاطَعَةِ، أُرِيدُ فَقَطْ أَنْ أُضِيفَ شَيْئًا: مَعَ صَدِيقِي شَرِيف أَتَعَلَّمُ المِصْرِيَّةَ مُنْذُ عَامٍ، وَهِيَ أَسْهَلُ لِي لِأَنَّنِي أَعْرِفُ الفُصْحَى.⁩
Sorry to interrupt, I just want to add one thing: with my friend Šarīf I've been studying Egyptian for a year, and it's easier for me because I know the fuṣḥā.
Laylā: Strong argument... you convinced me in half!
… ⁧نِصْفُ إِقْنَاعٍ يَكْفِينِي! وَبِالمُنَاسَبَةِ، أَنْتِ تَتَكَلَّمِينَ الآنَ بِالفُصْحَى⁩ : ⁧لُوكَا⁩ ⁧مِنْ أَجْلِي؟⁩
Half convinced enough for me! And by the way, now you speak in fuṣḥā...for me?
⁧لَيْلَى: طَبْعًا! لَوْ تَكَلَّمْتُ بِاللُّبْنَانِيَّةِ، لَكُنْتَ حَائِرًا تَمَامًا!⁩
LaylāOf course! If you spoke Lebanese, you would be completely lost!
⁧لُوكَا: مَفْهُومٌ. إِذَنِ اتَّفَقْنَا عَلَى شَيْءٍ وَاحِدٍ عَلَى الأَقَلِّ: الفُصْحَى لُغَةٌ مُشْتَرَكَةٌ مُفِيدَةٌ جِدًّا.⁩
Clear. Then we agree at least on one thing: the fuṣḥā is a very useful common language.

blocks.text: ⁧اِتَّفَقْنَا. وَالآنَ، مَاذَا نَطْلُبُ؟ أَنَا أُرِيدُ عَصِيرَ مَانْجُو!⁩ : ⁧لَيْلَى⁩ Laylā: All right. Now, what do we order? I want a mango juice!

What to notice. ⁧وَجْهًا لِوَجْهٍ⁩ • face to face • ⁧الكَلِمَاتُ الرَّسْمِيَّةُ⁩ Here are the official speeches. ⁧اِنْطِبَاع⁩ "Impression" is given. The courteous disagreement: ⁧لَا أَتَّفِقُ مَعَكَ تَمَامًا⁩ I do not entirely agree with you, ⁧أَفْهَمُ وِجْهَةَ نَظَرِكِ، لٰكِنْ⁩ I understand your point of view, but... ⁧عُذْرًا عَلَى المُقَاطَعَةِ⁩ I'm sorry to interrupt you. ⁧أَقْنَعْتَنِي نِصْفَ إِقْنَاعٍ⁩ You convinced me in half (absolute complement, B1-10). ⁧لَوْ تَكَلَّمْتُ⁩ … ⁧لَكُنْتَ⁩ ...unreal hypothetical period (B1-11). ⁧حَائِر⁩ "Perplexed, lost."
7. Okay or not.

rows: I completely agree · You're right · That's right
… ⁧هٰذَا صَحِيحٌ، وَلٰكِنْ⁩ · ⁧أَتَّفِقُ مَعَكَ إِلَى حَدٍّ مَا⁩
I agree to a certain extent · True, but...
I'm not sure · I don't know if...
I understand your point of view, but...
I do not agree at all · That is not true
You convinced me · Maybe you're right

blocks.text: The disagreement in Arab culture is often expressed by a positive introduction ( ⁧فِكْرَةٌ جَمِيلَةٌ، وَلٰكِنْ⁩ …; ⁧مَعَ احْتِرَامِي لِرَأْيِكَ⁩ ...) and rarely directly with older or in a higher position. A dry "no" sounds rude; A yes, but... it almost always works.
8. Fuṣḥā, dialect and Arabic spoken

rows: with an Arab from another country
fuṣḥā read with common dialect words
fuṣḥā; learn the words of his dialect
on the street, at the shop, at the cafe
dialect (EGY); If you freeze, fuṣḥā with Egyptian words
in an office, with a doctor
dialect with many words of fuṣḥā
courteous dialect; Technical terms in fuṣḥā

blocks.text: Mixing is not a mistake. All educated Arabs mix: a question in fuṣḥā can receive a reply in dialect, and a dialect phrase may contain a term of fuṣḥā. What matters is to remain understandable and courteous. However, avoid mixing within the same word or using the dialect in a formal writing (B1-22).
9. The Tabs-The Topic
On examination B1 (part E, oral) and in real conversations the same themes always return. Prepare for each one a card with 10 keywords, 3 ready phrases and 2 questions to ask the other.

rows: ⁧؟⁩ … ⁧مَا رَأْيُكَ فِي⁩ · ⁧هَلْ قَرَأْتَ خَبَرًا مُهِمًّا هٰذَا الأُسْبُوعَ؟⁩

blocks.text: Luca's work. Luca just says, ⁧أَعْمَلُ فِي الشُّرْطَةِ فِي مِيلَانُو⁩ , and he gladly talks about the human side of his work (contact with people, languages, colleagues). In conversations with strangers no one is required to give details about their work: a short and friendly answer and a change of topic ( ⁧وَأَنْتَ، مَاذَا تَعْمَلُ؟⁩ ) are completely normal.
10. Pronunciation

The rhythm of the conversation. In a conversation in fuṣḥā not all the endings are pronounced: we read \"in pause" the end of the groups of words. Focus on internal vowels, emphatic consonants and the intonation of questions (which rises to the end in questions yes/no: ⁧هَلْ تَتَكَلَّمُ الإِنْجِلِيزِيَّةَ؟⁩ ↗). The hesitations. ⁧يَعْنِي⁩ , ⁧فِي الحَقِيقَةِ⁩ , ⁧كَيْفَ أَقُولُ⁩ are pronounced by stretching the last vowel a bit (yaʿnīī...): it is the signal I'm thinking, I'm not finished.
11. New lexicon
★ ⁧مُدْهِش⁩ mudhiš amazing ⁧د ه ش⁩ active participle ⁧دَهْشَة⁩ Amazing (IV)
⁧سَخَّان⁩ saḫḫān water heater ⁧س خ ن⁩ name m.

Notes of use. ⁧فُوجِئْتُ بِـ⁩ I was surprised by the fact that it's much more natural than the ⁧فَاجَأَنِي⁩ In conversations: ⁧فُوجِئْتُ بِكَرَمِ النَّاسِ⁩ . ⁧أَقْنَعَ⁩ and ⁧اِقْتَنَعَ⁩ are the couple \"convincere / convince yourself": ⁧أَقْنَعَنِي⁩ → ⁧اِقْتَنَعْتُ⁩ . ⁧مُحْرِج⁩ It says of a situation: ⁧مَوْقِفٌ مُحْرِجٌ⁩ It's an awkward situation.

13. Exercises
Exercise 1 · Describe without naming

Explains in Arabic, without using the word (which you may not know), what it is: a) corkscrew · b) the umbrella · c) the charger · d) receipt · e) the hanger for clothes · f) passport · g) the air conditioner · h) the elevator
Exercise 2 · Ask and check

What do you say if: a) the other speaks too fast · b) you don't know a word he said · c) you want to check that you understand that the lesson is moved to Thursday · d) you didn't understand anything about the sentence · e) the other one misunderstands what you mean · f) You understand and you want to say it
Exercise 3 · Okay or not?

React to any claim with the grade given and add a topic: a) Cairo is too chaotic to live. b) Arabic is the most difficult language in the world. c) Studying with a teacher is better than on your own. d) Young people no longer read. e) The dialect is not necessary, just the fuṣḥā- (courtesy disagreement) f) The train is better than the plane.
Exercise 4 · Take time
Answer each question by starting with a formula to take time, then with an answer of two sentences:
a) ⁧مَا أَصْعَبُ شَيْءٍ فِي العَرَبِيَّةِ؟⁩ · b) ⁧لَوْ كُنْتَ وَزِيرًا لِلتَّعْلِيمِ، مَاذَا تُغَيِّرُ؟⁩ · c) ⁧مَا الفَرْقُ بَيْنَ الإِيطَالِيِّينَ وَالمِصْرِيِّينَ؟⁩ · d) ⁧أَيُّ⁩
⁧كِتَابٍ غَيَّرَ حَيَاتَكَ؟⁩

18. Oral production

1. The conversation (sessions) 1–4). Four sessions of 10–15 minutes with the tutor or Arabic partner, each on two section argument sheets 9. The tutor asks unexpected questions; you use at least five section strategies 3–7. Record sessions.

2. The debate. The tutor supports a thesis (e.g. the dialect before the fuṣḥā• • social media hurts more which is good ()); You disagree with me, you bring two arguments, and in the end you let yourself be half-convinced, or you convince him.
3. Two minutes without stopping. The tutor extracts a random argument; You talk two minutes without long breaks, using formulas to take time. If you miss a word, describe it.
